list.listitem: For patients with new-onset ascites, the initial test is a paracentesis with serum-ascitic albumin gradient (SAAG), cell count and total protein. C
If infection is suspected and/or paracentesis produces purulent ascitic fluid, culture ascitic fluid at bedside in blood culture bottles. C
Ascites is a marker of decompensated cirrhosis and, thus, indicates higher morbidity and mortality. B
First-line treatment of clinically-significant ascites in patients with cirrhosis is sodium restriction and diuresis with spironolactone with or without furosemide. B
Consider transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) in selected patients with refractory ascites. B
Liver transplant should be considered in patients with cirrhosis and ascites, especially refractory ascites. C
Serial therapeutic paracentesis or peritoneovenous shunt should be considered for patients with refractory ascites who are not candidates for TIPS or transplant. C

background.definition: Accumulation of excess fluid within the peritoneal cavity.

list.listitem: 5% to 10% of patients with compensated cirrhosis will develop ascites every year, representing about 80% of all abdominal effusions seen in clinical practice. Clincally evident ascites is the most common decompensating event in cirrhosis and carries the highest mortality rate.

Ascites occurred in 19.5% of a cohort of patients with hepatitis B or C followed for a mean of 7.7 years in an Italian study. See chapters on hepatitis B and hepatitis C for risk factors for those conditions.
Authors of a systematic review found an incidence rate of chylous ascites of up to 11% following major abdominal surgery, especially pancreatic surgery.
Refractory ascites (resistant to sodium restriction and diuretics) occurs in 10% of patients with cirrhosis.
Chronic liver disease and cirrhosis was the 12th leading cause of death in the United States in 2016, accounting for 40,367 deaths or 1.89% of total deaths.
Ascites is one of the 3 major markers of decompensated cirrhosis; the other markers are hepatic encephalopathy and portal hypertensive gastrointestinal bleeding.

Liver disorders that can lead to cirrhosis, and thereby ascites, include alcohol and drug-induced (eg, phenytoin, captopril, enalapril, isoniazid, statins) liver disease, infectious liver disease (eg, viral hepatitis, mononucleosis, cytomegalovirus), genetic liver disease (eg, Wilson's disease, hemochromatosis), autoimmune liver disease, liver cancer/metastatic disease, and primary biliary cirrhosis.
Hepatic resection, especially for hepatocellular carcinoma.
Right heart failure.
Nephrotic syndrome and after kidney transplant.
Pancreatitis.
Myxedema.
Many primary and metastatic cancers including hepatocellular carcinoma, melanoma, mesothelioma, and bladder and ovarian cancer.

Chyous ascites can result from lymphatic leakage from obstruction (eg, by tumor, trauma, tuberculosis, filariasis, congenital abnormalities), as a postoperative complication, or as a rare adverse effect of calcium channel blockers.
Infection, such as tuberculosis can cause exudative ascites.
Giant uterine leiomyoma.

In the setting of cirrhosis, portal hypertension and splanchnic vasodilation have multiple consequences. Those relevant to ascities are relative arterial underfilling resulting in the activation of vascoconstrictor and antidiuretic factors. The kidneys respond to this with sodium retention and plasma volume expansion.

Clinically significant portal hypertension (CSPH) is a high risk marker of decompensation. Historically determined by hepatic vein catheterization, now can be estimated using liver stiffness estimates , platelet count or, if needed, upper endoscopy.

Salt and water retention also occur in nephrotic syndrome; proteinuria causes hypoalbuminemia and resulting decreased intravascular oncotic pressure and leakage of extracellular fluid into the interstitium. Intravascular volume falls triggering the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone axis.
Lymphatic obstruction causes leakage of chylous fluid into the peritoneal cavity.
Direct peritoneal inflammation can be caused by tumor or infectious agents.

Non-selective beta blockers, especially carvedilol and in the setting of compensated cirrhosis with clinically significant portal hypertension (CSPF), can reduce the risk of decompensation, including ascities. C

Prevention of further liver damage in patients with cirrhosis may be helpful; these measures include avoiding alcohol (particularly in patients with hepatitis C or who have an alcohol component to their liver injury), limiting drug toxicity, treating liver infection, vaccinating against hepatitis A and B, and eating a nutritious diet that is low in salt and contains 1 to 1.5 g of protein per kilogram per day with vitamin supplementation in patients with muscle-wasting malnutrition. C

There is uncertainty about whether antibiotic primary prophylaxis against spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is beneficial outside of acute gastrointestinal bleeding. The American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (ASSLD) 2021 Practice Guidance notes the risk of multidrug resistance, antibiotic side effects and diminishing efficacy over time as concerns for long term primary prophylaxis. C

The benefits of nonselective beta blockers was demonstrated in an RCT of 201 Spanish patients with compensated portal hypertension without high-risk varices. Those randomized to a beta-blocker (67 to propranolol and 33 to carvedilol due to non-response to propranolol) had a significantly lower rate of decompensation or death than those on placebo (16% vs. 27% respectively) at a median follow-up of 37 months; this difference was primarily due to a lower rate of developing ascites (9% vs. 20%, respectively).
Abdominal distention with increased girth and bloating or bulging flanks, weight gain, and ankle swelling may be noted, as well as a fluid wave or shifting dullness on percussion. C

For patients with clinically apparent new onset ascites, the initial test is a paracentesis with evaluation of the ascitic fluid, including a serum-ascitic albumin gradient (SAAG), cell counts and total protein. History, physical, abdominal doppler ultrasound and assessments of the liver and renal function should be performed to guide additional assessments. C
If infection is suspected and/or paracentesis produces purulent ascitic fluid or positive Gram stain or the fluid should be cultured at the bedside in blood culture bottles. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Fatigue, nausea, jaundice, spider angiomas, elevated liver enzymes, history of alcohol abuse
Pedal edema, hepatomegaly, increased jugular venous distention, dyspnea
Upper abdominal pain radiating to the back, nausea, vomiting, elevated serum lipase

list.listitem: Abdominal distention with increased girth and bloating or bulging flanks, weight gain, and ankle swelling may be noted.

Ascites can sometimes be detected clinically by a fluid wave (LR+ 10) or shifting dullness (LR+ 6) on percussion; for the latter sign, the air-fluid interface is noted with the patient lying supine and when turned on the side, the line shifts upward. Clinical detection requires an accumulation of about 1500 mL.

Signs and symptoms of liver disease greatly increase the likelihood of ascites and include constitutional symptoms (eg, fatigue, weakness, nausea, vomiting), skin alterations (ie, jaundice [LR+ 3.38], palmar erythema, spider angiomas/telangiectasia [LR+ 54], excoriations, palpable purpura), right upper quadrant pain, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly (congestive splenomegaly from portal hypertension), gynecomastia, and testicular atrophy (hyperestrogenism).

Physical signs for specific liver diseases include Kayser-Fleischer rings (Wilson's disease); excessive skin pigmentation (hemochromatosis), and cachexia and firm hepatosplenomegaly (hepatocellular cancer).

Along with ascites, signs of more advanced liver disease are muscle wasting, lower extremity edema, dilated abdominal veins (caput medusa—collateral veins seen radiating from the umbilicus), bruising, asterixis (flapping of the hands when wrists are extended), congestive heart failure, and mental confusion or coma.

The initial test is a paracentesis with evaluation of the ascitic fluid to include a SAAG (Serum albumin ascites gradient, calculated by subtracting the ascitic fluid albumin from the serum albumin simultaneously obtained samples), cell count and total protein.

If the SAAG is greater than or equal to 1.1 g/dL, ascitic protein level should be assessed. If the ascitic protein is less than 2.5 g/dL, cirrhosis should be strongly suspected. Whereas if the ascitic protein is greater than or equal to 2.5 g/dL, a postsinusoidal etiology should be suspected and echocardiography and hepatic vein doppler performed.
If the SAAG is less than 1.1 g/dL, then peritoneal disease should be suspected. Considerations for ascitic fluid cytology, acid fast bacilli and abdominal imaging should be made.
If infection is suspected and/or paracentesis produces purulent ascitic fluid, or positive Gram stain, then the fluid should be cultured at the bedside in blood culture bottles. .
Testing serum for cancer antigen 125 (CA125) is not helpful in the differential diagnosis of ascites.
If malignant ascites is suspected, a minimum of 200 mL of fluid is suggested for removal and submission to cytopathology to increase sensitivity of the examination.

In one small case series, the probability of malignancy was 98% when omental thickening, thickening of the intestinal wall, and peritoneal implant were present together. US is also strongly recommended for use during drainage of ascites in the critical care setting.

In a study of 177 patients with ascites of unknown origin, use of FDG PET/CT had a sensitivity, specificity, and diagnostic accuracy of 92.3%, 83.6%, and 88.7%, respectively resulting in eventual diagnosis of 104 patients as having malignant ascites. Combination of imaging with assessment of tumor markers in ascitic fluid improved diagnostic accuracy slightly (90.4%).
A liver biopsy may be useful in diagnosing the underlying cause of liver disease.

For patients with clinically apparent new-onset ascites, the initial test is a paracentesis with evaluation of the ascitic fluid, including a serum-ascitic albumin gradient (SAAG), cell count, and differential and total protein.
In the setting of cirrhosis, ascites can be further classified as responsive, recurrent or refractory based on treatment response.
In patients with sudden decompensation, suspect hepatocellular carcinoma, portal vein thrombosis, or infection (eg, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis or tuberculosis).

The AASLD recommends moderate low sodium diet and gentle diuresis with spironolactone with or without furosemide as first-line treatments of clinically-significant ascites in patients with cirrhosis and a high SAAG (1.1 g/dL or more, reflecting portal hypertension). B
Alcoholic liver disease is dramatically affected by alcohol cessation including spontaneous resolution of ascites and/or increased responsiveness to medical therapy. B
Diuretic-sensitive patients should preferably be treated with sodium restriction and oral diuretics rather than serial paracentesis. C
Ascites in the setting of cirrhosis is an indication for referral to a transplant center for consideration of liver transplant. B

Refractory ascites, defined as ascites unresponsive to diet and diuretic treatment or rapidly recurring after paracentesis, is a unique clinical entity and should prompt a review of medications appropriateness and expedited referral to a liver transplant center. C

In addition to salt restriction (less than 2 g/day; see Other Treatment below), gentle diuresis with spironolactone (100-400 mg daily) with or without furosemide (40-160 mg daily) is used to control ascites.
Spironolactone alone appeared to be as effective as spironolactone with furosemide in a study of 100 patients with nonazotemic ascites.

In one small RCT, clonidine 0.075 mg twice daily begun 8 days before spironolactone use resulted in a shorter time for diuretic response, lower diuretic dose, fewer diuretic complications (eg, hyperkalemia, renal impairment), and decreased time to readmission for tense ascites.
Avoid use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs in patients with cirrhosis and ascites.

Use of angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers in patients with cirrhosis and ascites may be harmful as blood pressure is supported in these patients by elevated levels of vasoconstrictors such as angiotensin.

Use of non-selective beta-blockers does not affect survival or incidence of SBP or hepato-renal syndrome in patients with cirrhosis and ascites based on a review of 3 RCTs and 13 observational studies. Authors of a more recent meta-analysis of 8 observational studies also concluded that there is no difference in all-cause mortality with use of beta-blockers in patients with cirrhosis and ascites (38.6% with beta-blockers vs. 42.2% without beta-blockers).

In an Italian open-label RCT of 431 patients with decompensated cirrhosis receiving an anti-aldosteronic drug (eg, spironolactone) and furosemide, those randomized to albumin infusion (40 g twice weekly for 2 weeks, and then 40 g weekly for up to 18 months) had improved overall 18-month survival (77% vs. 66% for standard therapy alone, NNT = 9) and no decrease in quality-of life score compared to a decrease for those on standard therapy.
However, another RCT in hospitalized patients with cirrhosis found that a short duration series of infusions (daily for up to 14 days) did not improve outcomes.

A comparison of diuretics as opposed to paracentesis with albumin infusion in patients with tense ascites found greater benefit with paracentesis in eliminating ascites (96.5% vs. 72.8%), with fewer complications and no differences in readmission. However, a small study found that patients with cirrhosis treated by paracentesis who were not given spironolactone following the procedure reaccumulated fluid more often (93% vs. 18%).

Authors of a Cochrane review evaluating 49 RCTs with 3251 participants found significant uncertainty regarding the efficacy of transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) or aldosterone antagonists with or without loop diuretics, compared to paracentesis plus fluid replacement, to treat ascites among adults with decompensated liver cirrhosis and ascites. Based on very low-certainty evidence, it is unclear if treating ascites with TIPS or diuretics lowers mortality, adverse events, or liver transplantation compared to paracentesis plus fluid replacement.

Authors of a systematic review of treatment for malignant ascites found no RCTs; paracentesis had a temporary beneficial effect on symptoms, but data were inconsistent for use of diuretics and use of peritoneovenous shunting for control of ascites, and at significant risk.

In a large national hospital database study of 17,711 admissions for cirrhosis and ascites, in-hospital mortality was significantly reduced among patients who underwent paracentesis (6.5% vs. 8.5%); 61% of the total group underwent this procedure and the mean hospital stay was longer for these patients.

Serial therapeutic paracenteses may be performed in patients with refractory ascites. For large volume paracentesis, an albumin infusion of 6 to 8 g per liter of fluid removed appears to improve survival and is recommended by the AASLD guidelines. A small pilot study demonstrated midodrine orally was as effective as albumin infusion in reducing morbidity and mortality during large volume paracentesis and at a lower cost based.

Large volume paracentesis or long-term abdominal drains may be considered for palliative care of refractory ascites in end-stage liver disease. A small pilot RCT (n=36) suggests that costs and time in hospital are lower in the lon-term abdominal drain group compared with large volume paracentesis, but a larger study is needed.

A Cochrane review evaluating the efficacy of plasma expanders (eg, polygeline, dextrans, hydroxyethyl starch, IV infusion of ascitic fluid, crystalloids, or mannitol) administered after large volume paracentesis did not find any benefits or adverse events associated with their use, based on very low certainty evidence.
Portal hypertension can be managed with shunting in collaboration with a center with relevant expertise.

Authors of a Cochrane review found greater resolution of ascites at maximal follow-up with TIPS (HR 9.44; 95% CrI 1.93 to 62.68) compared to paracentesis plus fluid replacement based on very low-certainty evidence.

The advent of polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE)-covered stents, or "covered stents", may reduce the incidence of stent thrombosis and malfunction. However, a Cochrane review, based on low to very low-certainty evidence, found uncertain efficacy of covered stents over bare stents
A meta-analysis of 4 trials confirmed the above findings and also demonstrated a survival benefit (44% vs. 50% mortality).

A retrospective cohort study of 53 patients at a single institution found that TIPS could be performed in persons 65 and older, although complications were more common and mortality was slightly higher at 90 days than in younger patients (but not at 30 days and 1 year).
ASSLD recommends referral to a transplant center for patients with cirrhosis complicated by ascites, and expedited referral in the setting of refractory ascites.

A randomized trial found that outcomes were favorable for patients with malignant ascites due to colorectal cancer with cytoreductive surgery accompanied by hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy, and that the timing was not an important factor.
First-line treatment of ascites in patients with cirrhosis is sodium restriction (88 mmol or 2000 mg/day).

However, an RCT of salt restriction compared with unrestricted salt intake in patients with cirrhotic ascites demonstrated few differences, although the time for complete disappearance of ascites was shorter in patients with salt restriction and survival was significantly better for the subgroup of patients who did not have previous gastrointestinal bleeding.
In a multicenter RCT of 6 different treatments for ascites, salt restriction did not confer additional benefit to diuretic use.
Patients with ascites thought to have an alcoholic component should be counseled to abstain from alcohol consumption and treated for alcohol use disorder.
In the systematic review of chylous ascites, conservative treatment, including parenteral nutrition, was effective in nearly all cases.
Additional treatments such as allopurinol and branched-chain amino acids have limited data but may represent emerging therapies.

Suspect spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in patients with ascites who develop fever, abdominal pain, encephalopathy, renal failure, acidosis, or elevated WBC count. About 2.5% of hospitalizations in people with cirrhosis are for SBP.
Risk factors for development of SBP include upper GI bleeding, low ascitic protein concentration (< 1.5 g/dL), history of prior SBP, serum total bilirubin >2.5 mg/dL, and malnutrition.
Up to 1/3 of patients with SBP may only have encephalopathy or acute kidney injury, especialy if already hospitalized for other indications.

In one study, a scoring system using age (>60 years – 1 point), thrombocytopenia (≤100,000 cells/µL – 1 point), and CRP (>60 mg/L – 2 points) was helpful for predicting the presence of SBP. For patients with a score of 3 or 4, the positive predictive value for the diagnosis of SBP was 81.8% with a specificity of 98.8%; for those with a score of 0 or 1, the negative predictive value was 93.5% with a sensitivity of 87.9%.

Patients with ascitic fluid PMN counts greater than or equal to 250 cells/mm3 in a community-acquired setting, in the absence of recent B-lactam antibiotic exposure or known multidrug resistance, should receive empiric antibiotic therapy with cefotaxime 2 g every 8 hours or similar third generation cephalosporin. If there is known multidrug resistance, critical illness or the infection is nosocomial, carbapenems are recommended.

Oral ofloxacin (400 mg twice per day) can be considered as a substitute for IV cefotaxime in inpatients without prior exposure to quinolones, vomiting, shock, grade II (or higher) hepatic encephalopathy, or serum creatinine greater than 3 mg/dL.

A Cochrane review found considerable uncertainty regarding optimal antibiotic therapy for patients with SBP, citing significant methodological shortcomings among the 12 RCTs included in the network meta-analysis. A separate Cochrane review evaluating the effectiveness of antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent SBP in people with cirrhosis similarly found significant uncertainty regarding the efficacy of antibiotics and the most beneficial antibiotic regimen.

Patients being treated for SBP who also have a serum creatinine >1 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen >30 mg/dL, or total bilirubin >5 mg/dL should receive 1.5 g albumin per kg body weight within 6 hours of detection and 1.0 g/kg on day 3.
Hyponatremia is present in nearly half of patients with cirrhosis complicated by ascities. Over 20% of patients will have serum sodium values <130 mEq/L.
Similar to other hyponatremias, treatment depends on etiologies, symptoms, and acuity.
Serum sodium <130 mEq/L is a marker for increased risk of hepatic encephalopathy, hepatorenal syndrome, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis and mortality.
Fluid restriction is limited by patient tolerance as a restriction less than 1 liter per day is required for meaningful improvement in serum sodium.

Mild hyponatremia (Na 126-135 mEq/L) can be monitored and fluid restriction encouraged. Moderate Hyponatremia (120-125 mEq/L) should result in strict fluid restriction and, generally, continuation of diuretics.

For severe or acute symptomatic hyponatremia, in addition to fluid restriction, vaptans may be considered with caution and use limited to less than 30 days. Hypertonic saline may improve sodium but will worsen hypervolemia and ascities.
Abdominal wall and inguinal hernias are common in decompensated cirrhosis with ascites. Umbilical hernias develop in approximately 20% of such patients.
Ascities optimization and consideration for TIPS should be considered prior to surgery.

In a case-control study of patients undergoing umbilical hernia repair, morbidity and mortality rates for patients with ascites and/or esophageal varices were 13.1% and 5.1%, compared to 3.9% and 0.1% for the control group without these conditions. Predictors of adverse outcomes were age over 65 years, MELD score higher than 15, and albumin level less than 3.0 g/dL.
Chest tube insertion is contraindicated in patients with hepatic hydrothorax.

Therapy mirrors optimal management of ascites, first-line being dietary sodium restriction and diuretics, thoracentesis if needed for diagnostic purposes or significant dypsena, or consideration of TIPS if refractory.
Management of the following complications is nuanced and referral should be strongly considered.

Renal dysfunction due to circulatory dysfunction and renal vasoconstriction can occur in patients with cirrhosis and ascites; patients with hepatorenal syndrome (worsening azotemia, sodium retention, and oliguria without another identifiable cause) should have expedited referral for liver transplantation.
Albumin infusion plus administration of vasoactive drugs (eg, octreotide or midodrine) should be considered in the treatment of type 1 hepatorenal syndrome (HRS-1).

In one RCT of 196 patients with cirrhosis, ascites, and HRS-1, terlipressin plus albumin resulted in greater improvement in renal function vs. albumin alone although there were similar rates of HRS reversal. Based on low-quality evidence, a Cochrane review suggested that terlipressin may improve mortality and renal function among adults with cirrhosis and HRS-1, but acknowledged serious adverse events, hence concluded that better trials are needed.
A Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for TIPS for the treatment of adults with type 2 hepatorenal syndrome.

Acute portal vein thrombosis can occur in patients with decompensated cirrhosis resulting in recurrent upper gastrointestinal bleeding and refractory ascites. In one case series of 7 patients, use of fondaparinux 2.5 mg every 24 hours subcutaneously in the region of the umbilicus resulted in portal vein recanalization in 7 to 21 days in all patients with no recurrence at 1-month follow-up and no serious complications.
Ascites, as a marker of decompensated cirrhosis, drastically reduces median survival from over 15 years for compensated liver disease to approximately 1.5 years. B
Authors of a Cochrane review found that approximately 1 in 3 people with cirrhosis and ascites who received paracentesis and fluid replacement died within 11 months. B
In a cohort study of 100 patients with alcoholic cirrhosis (of whom 67% had ascites) followed for 15 years, the cumulative mortality rate was 49% at 1 year, 71% after 5 years, and 90% at 15 years. B

In one study of 30 patients with refractory ascites followed for a mean of 17.5 months, 25 developed renal dysfunction, with type-2 hepatorenal syndrome diagnosed in 16 (53%); survival was the same regardless of the type of dysfunction. B

In one cohort study, only 6 of 38 patients with end stage liver disease undergoing cardiopulmonary resuscitation survived to discharge. The presence of ascites did not predict survival, which was related to MELD score (≥20) and presence of a non-shockable rhythm. B

In a large cohort study of over 1 million patients undergoing intermediate or high-risk non-cardiac surgery, ascites was noted to be a risk factor for failure to rescue among those who experienced a perioperative myocardial infarction (adjusted OR 1.81, 95% CI 1.15-2.87). B

In a cohort study of 501 patients admitted over a 2-year study period, most for portal hypertensive bleeding and complicated ascites, predictors of 30-month survival were MELD score (hazard ratio (HR) 1.099), intensive care unit stay (HR 1.967) and bacterial infection (HR 2.226).

Ascites is a risk factor for multiple complications of cirrhosis, including spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, hyponatremia, and acute kidney injury including hepatorenal syndrome. It also predisposes the patient to malnutrition and the risk of sarcopenia, frailty, disability and poorer quality of life.

There are many conditions that cause hepatic cirrhosis in children that can lead to ascites. These include obstructive biliary disease (eg, biliary atresia, cystic fibrosis), infection (eg, viral hepatitis, toxoplasmosis, syphilis), vascular disease (eg, Rendu-Osler-Weber disease, Budd-Chiari syndrome), genetic disease (eg, Wilson's disease, glycogen storage disease, Gaucher disease), and drug-related disease (eg, methotrexate).
Similar to adults, lymphatic obstruction (of the thoracic duct within the abdomen) can cause ascites, secondary to a congenital anomaly, enlarged lymph nodes, or tumor.
